Name: group_convolution_bert
Title: Injecting BERT with group convolution
Motivation: BERT's attention blocks rely on heavy fully-connected layers, leading to high computational and memory costs. Replacing them with group convolution can reduce parameters and speed up inference without sacrificing representational power.
Method: We substitute the projection layers in each self-attention head with group convolutions. Features are split into groups, convolved with small kernels, then fed into the standard attention and normalization pipeline. This reduces parameter count and computation while maintaining accuracy.
Experiment: In this experiment, we compare the performance of different sentiment classification networks, especially considering using group convolution instead of fully connect layer in the attention block in BERT
Summary: Combine group convolution and BERT to improve the efficiency of BERT

Name: learned_sentiment_modulation_attention
Title: Learned Sentiment Modulation for Adaptive Attention in BERT
Motivation: Standard BERT attention mechanisms fail to dynamically adapt to the semantic impact of sentiment modifiers like negations and intensifiers. Humans readily adjust their interpretation based on these cues, suggesting a need for attention mechanisms that can learn to weigh contextually relevant information more effectively.
Method: We propose a Learned Sentiment Modulation (LSM) mechanism that enhances BERT's self-attention. For each input sequence, LSM first identifies tokens corresponding to predefined negation (e.g., 'not') and intensifier (e.g., 'very') words. For each identified modifier token, a specific linguistic feature representation is generated. Within each attention head, a small, *learnable* projection module takes this linguistic feature representation and outputs a scalar bias term. This bias term is then added to the raw attention scores computed for tokens that are modified by this specific linguistic cue *before* the softmax. This allows the model to learn the optimal way to adjust attention based on the type and presence of sentiment modifiers, leading to more nuanced and accurate sentiment representations. The novelty lies in the integration of learned, adaptive bias terms directly into the attention score calculation, conditioned on identified sentiment modifiers.
Experiment: 1. Define lists of common negation and intensifier words. 2. For each modifier token, create a feature representation (e.g., one-hot encoding of type). 3. Subclass `BertForSequenceClassification` to create `LearnedSentimentModulatedBert`. Modify the attention layer's forward pass: identify modifier tokens, generate their feature representations, use a learnable projection module per head to output a bias term conditioned on the modifier type, and add this bias to the attention scores before softmax. 4. Update `BertClassifier` to use this new custom BERT model. 5. Train and evaluate the modified model using the existing `BertTrainer` on the SST-2 dataset. 6. Compare performance (accuracy, AUC) against a baseline BERT model. 7. Analyze the learned bias terms and attention patterns to understand how the model adapts.
Summary: Introduces a Learned Sentiment Modulation mechanism that allows BERT's attention to adaptively adjust based on learned biases derived from negation and intensifier words.
